sheets.name: Ring now
sheets.intro: Ring 000 for any of the first six. You will never be told off for ringing. Trust what you are seeing.

rows.label: Ring 000: not breathing, or fighting to breathe
rows.value: Gasping, grunting with every breath, ribs sucking in, head bobbing, or long pauses. Ring 000 now.

rows.label: Ring 000: blue or grey lips, tongue or face
rows.value: Any blue or grey around the mouth or on the tongue, or skin gone grey or mottled. Ring 000 now.

rows.label: Ring 000: a fit or convulsion
rows.value: Jerking, stiffening, or staring and unresponsive. Lay them on their side and ring 000.

rows.label: Ring 000: unresponsive, floppy or will not wake
rows.value: Limp like a rag doll, or you cannot rouse them properly. Ring 000 now.

rows.label: Ring 000: a rash that does not fade when pressed
rows.value: Press a clear glass on it. Red or purple spots that stay put can be meningococcal. Ring 000 now.

rows.label: Ring 000: choking, a bad fall, or a head knock
rows.value: Also any drowning, burn, or a swallowed object, medicine or chemical. Ring 000 now.

rows.label: Any fever under 3 months old
rows.value: 38C or over, measured under the arm, is an emergency department trip now. Do not wait it out.

rows.label: Cold, pale or mottled, or shivering
rows.value: A newborn who has gone cold and pale can be as unwell as a hot one. Be seen today.

rows.label: Signs of dehydration
rows.value: Fewer wet nappies, dry mouth, no tears, a sunken soft spot, or sleepy and hard to feed. Be seen today.

rows.label: A cry that sounds wrong
rows.value: High pitched, moaning, weak, or hours of inconsolable screaming that is not their normal. Ring today.

rows.label: Refusing feeds, or vomiting every feed
rows.value: Two or three feeds refused or thrown straight back up, or green or bloody vomit. Be seen today.

rows.label: Yellow skin on day one, or deepening jaundice
rows.value: Yellow in the first 24 hours, or spreading to the tummy, legs or whites of the eyes. Ring today.

rows.label: A bulging or sunken soft spot
rows.value: The fontanelle should sit flat and soft. Tight and bulging, or dipped in, needs seeing today.

rows.label: Blood in the nappy, or a swollen hard tummy
rows.value: Blood in poo or vomit, a tight tummy, or no poo at all with vomiting. Be seen today.

rows.label: You just know something is wrong
rows.value: Your gut is a real symptom. Ring your nurse line, MCH or GP, or go in. Say what has changed.

asks: Say the age in weeks first: under three months changes everything.
Tell them the temperature, how many wet nappies, and when the last feed was.
Ask what would make you need to come straight back.
Ask them to watch you feed before you leave.

sheets.name: Safe sleep setup
sheets.intro: Red Nose has the final say on sleep. Run this list every time you put them down, awake or asleep.

rows.label: On the back, every sleep
rows.value: Back for every nap and every night, from day one. Not the side, not the tummy.

rows.label: Face uncovered
rows.value: No hats indoors, no hoods, no bibs, no dummy chains, nothing over the head or face.

rows.label: Their own safe cot
rows.value: A cot that meets the Australian standard. Not a couch, a beanbag, a pram or your bed.

rows.label: In your room for 6 to 12 months
rows.value: Same room as you, their own cot, for the first six to twelve months. It is the easy win.

rows.label: Firm, flat, clean mattress
rows.value: Firm and flat, snug to the cot sides, no gaps a hand can fit in. No tilts or wedges.

rows.label: Feet to the foot of the cot
rows.value: Slide them down so their feet touch the end, then tuck bedding in no higher than the chest.

rows.label: Nothing loose in the cot
rows.value: No pillows, doonas, bumpers, positioners, toys or soft cot liners. Flat and boring is safest.

rows.label: Smoke free, before and after birth
rows.value: No smoking or vaping in the house, the car or near them. This one matters more than most.

rows.label: Not too hot
rows.value: Dress them for the room, roughly what you need plus one light layer. Check the chest or back of the neck.

rows.label: Safe wrap or a fitted sleeping bag
rows.value: Arms free once they stir at night. Stop wrapping the moment they show any sign of rolling.

rows.label: Never sleep on a couch or chair with them
rows.value: Couch or armchair sleep is the highest risk setup there is. Move to the bed or the cot.

rows.label: If they fall asleep on you
rows.value: Pop them in the cot on their back when you can. If you are drowsy, hand them over first.

asks: Ring the Red Nose line on 1300 998 698 to talk through your actual room and cot.
Ask your MCH nurse to check the cot setup at the home visit.
Ask what to change the day they start rolling.

sheets.name: The 2am run
sheets.intro: Same order every time. Boring and dark is the whole trick: you are teaching night from day.

rows.label: 1. Lights stay low
rows.value: One dim lamp or a warm nightlight. No overheads, no phone screen in their face.

rows.label: 2. Barely talk
rows.value: Whisper or stay quiet. No chat, no games, no eye contact games. Night is not fun time.

rows.label: 3. Offer the feed first
rows.value: Hungry is the usual answer. Feed before you unwrap or change, unless the nappy has leaked.

rows.label: 4. Change only if you need to
rows.value: Poo, a leak or sore skin means change. A plain wet nappy overnight can often wait.

rows.label: 5. Burp and rewrap
rows.value: Upright on your shoulder for a minute or two, then wrap or zip them back up, arms as before.

rows.label: 6. Back in the cot, on the back
rows.value: Down drowsy if you can, on the back, feet to the foot of the cot, face clear.

rows.label: 7. Hand on the chest, then out
rows.value: Steady hand, a shhh, then leave. Give them a few minutes to grumble themselves down.

rows.label: 8. Still unsettled after a while
rows.value: Try again: nappy, wind, too hot or cold, suck, or a quiet cuddle. Then reset and repeat.

rows.label: 9. Hand over and write it down
rows.value: Note the time and side or amount, say it out loud to the other one, then swap shifts.

rows.label: 10. Swap so each of you gets one long block
rows.value: Split the night into halves rather than both waking. Four hours unbroken beats eight broken.

rows.label: If you feel yourself losing it
rows.value: Put them safely in the cot, shut the door and breathe for a few minutes. That is the safe choice.

rows.label: Never bring them to a couch to feed when tired
rows.value: If you might doze off, feed sitting up in bed with the bedding clear, or wake the other one.

asks: Ask your MCH nurse to watch a feed and check the latch if nights are getting worse.
Ask the ABA helpline about night feeds and supply on 1800 686 268.
Ask your GP about sleep and mood at the six week check.

sheets.name: Yes, that is normal
sheets.intro: Newborns are loud, twitchy and leaky. Here is the stuff that looks alarming and is not.

rows.label: Hiccups, constantly
rows.value: A few times a day is normal and does not bother them. No treatment, they grow out of it.

rows.label: Sneezing a lot
rows.value: Clearing out fluff and dust from tiny nostrils. Sneezing on its own is not a cold.

rows.label: Snuffly, rattly breathing
rows.value: Narrow noses make noise. Fine if they are feeding well and the chest is not working hard.

rows.label: Startling with arms flung out
rows.value: The startle reflex. A snug wrap with the hips free settles it. It fades over a few months.

rows.label: Grunting, groaning and straining
rows.value: They grunt in their sleep and strain to poo. Soft poo when it arrives means all is well.

rows.label: Irregular breathing while asleep
rows.value: Fast, then slow, then a pause of a few seconds. Even colour and easy breaths mean it is fine.

rows.label: Posseting after feeds
rows.value: A small milky spill with a burp, most feeds. Weight gain and happy baby means no action.

rows.label: Mustard yellow, seedy poo
rows.value: From about day five on breastmilk. Can be green, lumpy or explosive and still be normal.

rows.label: Cluster feeding, usually at night
rows.value: Feed, doze, feed again for hours, often early evening. It builds your supply, it is not failure.

rows.label: Crying peaking at 6 to 8 weeks
rows.value: Crying climbs to a peak around six to eight weeks, then eases. Nothing you did caused it.

rows.label: Spots, blotches and peeling skin
rows.value: Milia, baby acne and flaky skin in the first weeks all pass on their own. Leave them alone.

rows.label: Weight dip in the first week
rows.value: Losing some birth weight then gaining it back by about two weeks is expected.

rows.label: When any of this changes the answer
rows.value: Fever, hard work to breathe, a rash that will not fade, projectile or green vomit, fewer wet nappies.

asks: Ask your MCH nurse to weigh them if you are unsure about feeding.
Ask your GP whether reflux is worth looking at if they spill and are miserable.
Ask what your nearest after hours option is, before you need it.

sheets.name: Wet nappy count
sheets.intro: Wet nappies are the best proof they are getting enough. Count them, do not guess.

rows.label: Day 1
rows.value: 1 or more wet nappy. Poo is black, sticky meconium. Colostrum comes in tiny amounts, and that is right.

rows.label: Day 2
rows.value: 2 or more wet nappies. Still meconium. Feed often, at least eight to twelve times in 24 hours.

rows.label: Day 3
rows.value: 3 or more wet nappies. Poo turning greenish brown as your milk comes in.

rows.label: Day 4
rows.value: 4 or more wet nappies, getting heavier. Poo going yellow and looser.

rows.label: Day 5 onwards
rows.value: 5 or more heavy wet nappies every 24 hours, pale wee, and 3 or more soft yellow poos a day.

rows.label: How heavy is heavy enough
rows.value: A wet disposable has real weight to it. Tip three tablespoons of water into a dry one to learn the feel.

rows.label: After about 6 weeks, fewer poos
rows.value: Breastfed babies can go days between poos and still be fine, as long as wet nappies hold up.

rows.label: Pink or orange brick dust in the nappy
rows.value: Common in the first days. If it is still showing after day three, ring your nurse or GP.

rows.label: 4 or fewer heavy wet nappies after day 5
rows.value: Ring your MCH nurse, GP or your state nurse line today. Keep offering feeds while you wait.

rows.label: No wet nappy at all for 6 hours
rows.value: Ring today. With a dry mouth, a sunken soft spot or a sleepy baby, go to the emergency department.

rows.label: Dark, strong smelling wee, or dry nappies
rows.value: Dark concentrated wee means not enough fluid in. Ring your nurse line or GP today.

rows.label: No poo at all by day 3, or blood in poo
rows.value: Also white or chalky poo, or poo still black after day four. Be seen today.

asks: Ask the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268 if you are worried about supply.
Ask your MCH nurse for a weigh in and a feed assessment.
Ask whether your baby needs reviewing if weight gain has stalled.

sheets.name: First 48 hours home
sheets.intro: You will not remember any of this, so here is the order. Nothing on this list is optional or hard.

rows.label: 1. Car seat in, then straight inside
rows.value: Take them out of the capsule as soon as you are in. Capsules are for travel, not for sleeping in.

rows.label: 2. Set the cot up now
rows.value: Firm flat mattress, nothing loose, in your room. Do it before you are too tired to think.

rows.label: 3. Lock the phone numbers in
rows.value: 000, your nurse line, MCH, GP and the hospital, saved in both phones before the first night.

rows.label: 4. Feed on demand, day and night
rows.value: Eight to twelve feeds in 24 hours, whenever they cue. Wake them to feed if four hours have passed.

rows.label: 5. Start the nappy and feed tally
rows.value: Scrappy notes on paper or your phone. Times, sides or amounts, wets and poos. It saves phone calls.

rows.label: 6. Keep the cord stump dry
rows.value: Nappy folded below it, clean with water only if it is dirty, let air at it. It drops off in one to three weeks.

rows.label: 7. Skip the bath
rows.value: Top and tail with warm water instead. A real bath can wait days, and twice a week is plenty.

rows.label: 8. Expect the midwife or MCH visit
rows.value: Usually day one to five after you get home. Write your questions on the fridge as they occur to you.

rows.label: 9. Sleep when they sleep, properly
rows.value: One of you lies down while the other holds the baby. Visitors and tidying come well after this.

rows.label: 10. Eat, drink, and keep water where you feed
rows.value: A bottle of water and one handed food at every feeding spot. Feeding is thirsty work.

rows.label: 11. Watch for yellow skin
rows.value: Jaundice often shows on day two to four. Press a finger on the nose or chest and look as it refills.

rows.label: 12. Book the first GP check
rows.value: Around one to two weeks, plus the six to eight week check and immunisations. Book it now.

rows.label: Anything on the Ring now sheet
rows.value: Breathing trouble, blue or grey, a fit, a fever, a non fading rash, floppy. Ring 000 or go in.

asks: Ask who to ring overnight in your area, and write the number down.
Ask the nurse to watch a full feed and check the latch.
Ask what weight gain they want to see by the next visit.

sheets.name: Who to ring
sheets.intro: Save these in both phones tonight. None of them mind being rung, and none of them judge.

rows.value: Ambulance, police, fire. Breathing trouble, blue or grey, a fit, floppy, a rash that will not fade.

rows.label: Poisons Information 13 11 26
rows.value: 24 hours, Australia wide. Swallowed medicine, a cleaning product, a plant, or a double dose.

rows.label: healthdirect 1800 022 222
rows.value: 24 hour nurse line for most of Australia. Should we be seen, and where should we go.

rows.label: 13 HEALTH 13 43 25 84 (QLD)
rows.value: Queensland's 24 hour nurse and health advice line. Same job as healthdirect.

rows.label: Nurse on Call 1300 60 60 24 (VIC)
rows.value: Victoria's 24 hour registered nurse line for health advice when the GP is shut.

rows.label: Maternal and Child Health Line 13 22 29 (VIC)
rows.value: 24 hours, for feeding, sleep, crying and settling. Your first call for anything not urgent.

rows.label: Your MCH or child health nurse
rows.value: The free, local, non urgent one. Weights, feeding, sleep, your own head. Book or drop in.

rows.label: Your GP
rows.value: Fevers, rashes, reflux, jaundice, the one to two week and six to eight week checks, immunisations.

rows.label: ABA Breastfeeding Helpline 1800 686 268
rows.value: 24 hours, staffed by trained counsellors. Latch, supply, blocked ducts, pain, weaning, bottles.

rows.label: Pregnancy, Birth and Baby 1800 882 436
rows.value: 7am to midnight, 7 days. Maternal child health nurses for any question about the first year.

rows.label: Red Nose 1300 998 698
rows.value: Safe sleep advice, and bereavement support. Ring them about your actual cot and room setup.

rows.label: PANDA 1300 726 306
rows.value: Perinatal anxiety and depression, for both of you. Mon to Fri, and Saturdays. Ring early, not late.

rows.label: Lifeline 13 11 14
rows.value: 24 hours. If you are in crisis, cannot cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself or the baby.

rows.label: 13YARN 13 92 76
rows.value: 24 hours, for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who need to talk to a mob who get it.

rows.label: 1800RESPECT 1800 737 732
rows.value: 24 hours, family violence and sexual assault support. If home does not feel safe, ring them.

asks: Ask your hospital for its after hours maternity or newborn number before discharge.
Ask your MCH nurse which local service covers nights and weekends.
Ask your GP practice what to do when they are closed.
